title: Payment API returning HTTP 503 after Redis pool exhaustion
alert_text: Payment API is returning HTTP 503 on /v1/charges. Error rate 34% and climbing.
root_cause: Redis connection pool exhaustion: a leaked connection in the charge-capture path held sockets under load, so new requests waited for a free connection until the pool timed out and the API returned 503.
resolution: Hotfix the connection leak (return connection to pool in finally block), raise the Redis pool size from 10 to 50, and restart the affected workers.
outcome: Service recovered in ~15 minutes after deploy. Error rate back to baseline <0.1%.
lessons: Redis connection-pool exhaustion on payment-api presents as HTTP 503 with 'pool timed out' in logs.
A 503 that climbs gradually with traffic points to resource exhaustion, not a bad deploy.

title: Orders service database connection pool exhausted after deploy
alert_text: Orders service is timing out. Postgres max_connections reached, connection wait queue growing.
root_cause: A deploy halved the connection reuse in the ORM configuration, so every request opened a new Postgres connection. Postgres hit max_connections (200) and started refusing new sessions.
resolution: Reverted the ORM pool config, enabled pgbouncer transaction pooling, restarted the orders deployment.
outcome: Connections stabilized within 10 minutes of rollback. Added max_connections alerting.
lessons: After any orders-service deploy, check Postgres connection count first.
Postgres max_connections exhaustion shows as 500s plus 'too many clients already' in logs.

title: Checkout service memory leak causing OOM restarts
alert_text: Checkout pods restarting repeatedly. Container memory at 98% of limit.
root_cause: Unbounded in-process cart cache introduced in the January release: entries were never evicted, so heap grew with unique sessions until the container exceeded its memory limit and was OOM-killed.
resolution: Replaced the in-process cache with the shared Redis cache and set a 30-minute TTL. Rolled pods one at a time.
outcome: Memory flatlined at ~60% of limit. Added memory-growth alert per deployment.
lessons: Checkout-service memory that climbs steadily across hours means the cart cache, not a traffic spike.
OOM restart loops on checkout-service have happened twice; both were in-process caching bugs.

title: API gateway returning 504 after upstream timeout regression
alert_text: API gateway 504s at 12% across all routes. Latency p99 above 30s.
root_cause: The search-team deployment increased their p99 to 28s; the gateway timeout was 30s, so a large fraction of proxied requests hit the gateway deadline and returned 504.
resolution: Raised the gateway route timeout to 45s as an interim fix and the search team reverted the slow query. Added per-route timeout dashboards.
outcome: 504 rate dropped to zero after the search revert; timeout change kept as headroom.
lessons: Gateway-wide 504s are usually a slow upstream, not a gateway fault. Check the slowest upstream first.
The gateway timeout budget is 30s; any upstream p99 near that will surface as 504s.

title: Auth service token validation failing after certificate expiry
alert_text: All authenticated requests returning 401. Login and token refresh broken.
root_cause: The internal signing certificate expired at 04:00 UTC and the service rejected every token signature, returning 401 for all authenticated traffic.
resolution: Rotated the signing certificate immediately, deployed the renewed trust bundle, and added expiry monitoring with 14/7/2-day alerts.
outcome: Full recovery by 04:48. Cert rotation automated afterwards.
lessons: Sudden 100% 401 rate with 'certificate verify failed' in logs = expired certificate, not a code bug.
Auth-service certificates expire quarterly; check the expiry dashboard when auth breaks.

title: Notification consumer lag from unbounded retry queue
alert_text: Notification delivery delayed by 20+ minutes. Kafka consumer lag growing linearly.
root_cause: An email provider outage caused every send to fail and be requeued without a backoff, so the retry topic grew until the consumer fell minutes behind real traffic.
resolution: Added exponential backoff and a dead-letter queue for repeated failures, reprocessed the backlog after the provider recovered.
outcome: Lag drained in 40 minutes after backoff fix. DLQ alerting added.
lessons: Consumer lag on notification-service usually means a downstream provider outage, not a consumer bug.
Check the retry topic depth before restarting consumers; restarts without backoff made it worse.

title: Payment API latency spike from missing database index
alert_text: Payment API p99 latency jumped from 200ms to 8s. Error rate normal.
root_cause: The monthly reporting job started after a schema change dropped the created_at index on charges; its full-table scans saturated the database IO budget and slowed the whole API.
resolution: Recreated the index concurrently, moved the reporting job to the read replica, and staggered its schedule.
outcome: Latency back under 300ms within minutes of index creation.
lessons: On payment-api, latency spikes with a normal error rate are database-side; check slow queries before services.
Schema migrations on charges can silently drop indexes used by the reporting job.

title: Search service degraded by Elasticsearch shard rebalancing
alert_text: Search queries 5-10x slower. Elasticsearch cluster yellow, shards relocating.
root_cause: A data node was replaced, triggering automatic shard rebalancing; heavy shard recovery IO starved query threads and degraded search latency cluster-wide.
resolution: Temporarily throttled rebalancing, enabled replica shard allocation during a low-traffic window, and re-enabled normal speed after recovery.
outcome: Search latency recovered once rebalancing finished during low traffic.
lessons: Search-service latency degradation often coincides with cluster maintenance or node replacement.
Check shard relocation status before debugging query performance.

title: Deployment failure from misconfigured environment variables
alert_text: Checkout deploy to staging failed health checks and rolled back automatically.
root_cause: A required PAYMENT_PROVIDER_URL variable was missing from the staging environment config, so the app aborted on startup validation and failed every health check.
resolution: Added the missing variable to the deploy config, hardened startup validation to fail fast with explicit messages, and added a config checklist to the deploy template.
outcome: Staging deploy healthy on the next run; template updated to prevent recurrence.
lessons: A crash-loop right after deploy with startup validation errors means missing environment config, not bad code.
Checkout-service staging deploys need the PAYMENT_PROVIDER_URL variable present.

title: Rate limiter misconfiguration blocking legitimate traffic
alert_text: Gateway returning 429 for a major customer. Traffic patterns look normal.
root_cause: A new per-route limit was configured per-IP instead of per-API-key; a customer whose traffic is NAT'd through few IPs exhausted the threshold in minutes.
resolution: Switched the route's limiter to per-API-key, raised the limit for that tier, and raised a config-review requirement for limiter changes.
outcome: 429s stopped immediately after the config fix.
lessons: Gateway 429s affecting a single customer are limiter config, not an attack — check which dimension the limiter keys on.
Per-IP limits break NAT'd enterprise customers; use per-API-key for paid tiers.

title: Inventory service deadlock under flash-sale load
alert_text: Inventory API timing out during flash sale. Lock wait timeouts in the database.
root_cause: The flash-sale reservation path locked inventory rows in inconsistent order across code paths, producing circular waits that Postgres resolved as deadlocks under high concurrency.
resolution: Enforced consistent row-lock ordering in the reservation path, added deadlock retry logic, and load-tested the sale flow.
outcome: Flash sale completed with error rate under 0.2%.
lessons: Inventory-service timeouts that start with a sales event are database deadlocks in the reservation path.
'deadlock detected' in Postgres logs plus traffic spikes confirms it; retry logic handles the residual.

title: Payment API 503 during Kubernetes node autoscaling event
alert_text: Brief 503 burst on Payment API. Several pods rescheduled at once.
root_cause: A cluster node was drained for maintenance; payment-api pods rescheduled together and the surge of cold-start readiness probes momentarily reduced serving capacity below demand.
resolution: Configured a pod disruption budget requiring at least 3 replicas available, spread pods across zones with anti-affinity, and scheduled node maintenance in off-peak windows.
outcome: Subsequent node drains caused no customer-visible errors.
lessons: Short 503 bursts on payment-api during a node drain are a disruption-budget gap, not an app bug.
Payment-api needs a PDB of min 3 available replicas and zone anti-affinity.

title: Analytics warehouse query storm starving the primary database
alert_text: Orders service latency spiked at 2 AM. Long-running queries from analytics on the primary.
root_cause: A scheduled analytics dashboard refresh ran six heavy aggregate queries against the production primary at 02:00, saturating CPU and starving order writes.
resolution: Pointed all analytics queries at the read replica, added a statement timeout for analytics roles, and rescheduled the refresh.
outcome: No impact on order traffic after cutover to the replica.
lessons: Overnight latency degradation on orders-service is usually analytics queries on the primary; check pg_stat_activity first.
Analytics roles must run against the read replica with a statement timeout.

title: Notification service provider 429s slowing email delivery
alert_text: Email notifications delayed. Upstream email provider returning 429.
root_cause: A marketing campaign tripled email volume beyond the provider plan's rate limit; the provider throttled sends with 429s and the queue grew.
resolution: Enabled provider rate-limit-aware sending with adaptive throttling, split transactional and marketing traffic across two provider accounts.
outcome: Delivery latency normalized; campaign volume handled by the second account.
lessons: Notification-service delays during marketing campaigns are provider rate limits; check upstream 429 counts.
Marketing traffic must be throttled separately from transactional email.

title: Redis cluster failover causing transient session errors
alert_text: Checkout errors for ~5 minutes. Redis replicas promoting, connection resets in logs.
root_cause: A Redis primary failed and the cluster promoted a replica; clients with long-lived connections reset during the failover window and sessions could not be re-established until clients reconnected.
resolution: Enabled client-side connection retry with jittered backoff, shortened Redis client timeouts, and validated session recovery on failover in staging.
outcome: A later unplanned failover produced no customer-visible errors.
lessons: Transient checkout errors with 'connection reset by peer' against Redis indicate a failover, not an outage.
Checkout-service Redis clients need retry-with-backoff enabled to survive failovers.
